blocks.content: kubectl logs is usually the first command reached for when a Pod is misbehaving, showing exactly what the application inside actually printed, before anything else is investigated.
When a Pod looks wrong, its logs are almost always the fastest place to find out why, exactly the same instinct covered for docker logs throughout the Docker course, applied here at the Pod level.

blocks.alt: The same first instinct as Docker logs, applied to a Kubernetes Pod

blocks.content: -f follows the log output live, streaming new lines as they are produced, the standard way to watch a Pod behave in real time while reproducing an issue.

blocks.alt: Streamed output, watched live, as an issue is actively reproduced

blocks.content: This is genuinely important, and easy to miss, if a container has already crashed and restarted, its current logs start fresh, empty of anything from before the crash. --previous retrieves the logs from that last, terminated instance instead, exactly what you need when investigating a CrashLoopBackOff (covered fully in the Troubleshooting module).

blocks.alt: The logs from before the crash, not the empty logs of the fresh restart

blocks.content: 4. Choosing a Container in a Multi-Container Pod
blocks.text: 4. Choosing a Container in a Multi-Container Pod

blocks.content: As covered in the Multi-Container Pods topic, a single Pod can hold several containers, -c specifies exactly which one's logs you want, without it, kubectl logs does not know which container you mean.

blocks.alt: A required flag, the moment a Pod holds more than one container

blocks.content: A real debugging session commonly combines these, following logs live during a reproduction attempt, then checking --previous logs after an actual crash, exactly the practical toolkit this command provides.

blocks.alt: The practical toolkit this one command actually provides, combined as needed

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl logs is usually the first debugging step, -f follows output live, --previous retrieves logs from a crashed instance before it restarted.
-c is required to pick a specific container in a multi-container Pod, without it the command has no way to know which one you mean.
